outcome: No proof, disproof, counterexample, or scope-changing result found since 26 January 2024; the only within-window developments are continued computational verification (OEIS A005235 extended to the first 4600 primorials, as of August 2026, all prime) and an AI-agent-generated GitHub issue merely proposing a Lean formalization of the conjecture's statement (April 2026), not a proof attempt.

summary: Fortune's conjecture (no Fortunate number is composite) remains open, with no result in the 26 Jan 2024–present window that changes the stated question. Three lines of activity exist. (1) Computational verification continues: OEIS A005235's data page shows a comment dated August 2026 (attributed to Brock Falfas) stating the first 4600 primorials have been checked and all corresponding Fortunate numbers are prime, extending the prior record of ~3000 (2017) / ~4600 terms already noted by the triage. Per the rules in §3.1, extending a verification record on an existence-type statement ('is there a composite Fortunate number') narrows where a counterexample could hide but does not answer the question, so this is not scope-changing progress on the conjecture itself — it is the routine continuation of a decades-long computational check, and I do not code it as `progress`. (2) A GitHub issue (#3688) was opened 2 April 2026 in Google DeepMind's formal-conjectures repository by user franzhusch, proposing to add a Lean/Mathlib formalization of the conjecture's *statement* (not a proof or disproof). Its footer states plainly: 'This issue was generated by an AI agent and reviewed by me' — this is AI involvement in tracking/formalization overhead only, producing no mathematics that bears on the truth of the conjecture, so ai_role is `none` per the formalisation_only rule (§6.2), even though I record the quote and mark formalisation_only true for completeness. (3) A partial/computational-evidence paper by Hayat Rezgui ('New explorations and remarkable inequalities related to Fortune's conjecture and fortunate numbers', Refaad) is dated 20 December 2023 — before the frozen revision's 26 January 2024 cutoff — so even though it proves the conjecture 'in a particular case' by two methods and verifies an inequality across the first 3000 known terms, it is out of the window entirely (open_stale territory would apply only if it were the sole basis for a status change, which it is not, since it predates the window and no later paper restates or extends it). No AI system is mentioned in that paper. I found no arXiv preprints, no lab announcements, and no expert digestions of any new proof or disproof attempt in the window. The conjecture is coded `open` with `no_change_found` true.
competing_reading: One could argue the continued OEIS verification (2017's ~3000 terms to 2026's 4600 terms) constitutes 'progress' in a loose sense, since it is new computational work performed within the window. But per §3.1's explicit rule that record-extension on an infinitude/existence-type question is not scope-changing progress unless the record itself is the question (which it is not here — the question is whether a composite Fortunate number exists, not what the largest verified term is), I classify this as no_change_found rather than `progress`. A stricter reading might also want a `partial` credit for the Rezgui paper if one dates it to a later re-publication or indexing date rather than the original December 2023 preprint/publication date; I found no evidence of any 2024+ re-publication, so I keep it fully outside the window.
what_would_settle_it: A published proof or disproof of the general conjecture; a discovered composite Fortunate number (which would refute it); or, short of that, any peer-reviewed/expert-digested advance restricting composite Fortunate numbers to a provably finite or empty set. Also relevant: confirmation of whether the Rezgui paper's December 2023 date is a preprint date only, with a later 2024+ formal publication date that might bring it into the window (I found no evidence of this).
